title: Exponents and Exponential Functions
bigQuestion: What happens when a quantity multiplies by the same factor again and again, and how can we predict where it ends up?

story.title: The Penny That Beat a Million Dollars
story.kicker: Offered a choice between a fortune and a penny that doubles, most people choose wrong.
paragraphs: Imagine a stranger makes you an offer. Option one: one million dollars in cash, right now. Option two: a single penny today, two pennies tomorrow, four the next day, and so on, doubling every day for 30 days. You keep only what you receive on day 30. Most people laugh and take the million. A penny is a penny, and 30 days is not very long.

Follow the pennies for a while and the laugh seems fair. Day 1 is $0.01. Day 5 is $0.16. Day 10 is $5.12, about the price of a sandwich. By day 15 you would receive $163.84. After two full weeks the doubling penny cannot buy a used bicycle. The million dollars looks safe.

Then the doubling starts to bite. Day 20 pays $5,242.88. Day 25 pays $167,772.16. Day 28 pays $1,342,177.28, and the million has already been passed. Day 30 pays $5,368,709.12. Nothing about the rule changed. The same instruction, multiply by 2, was followed every day. What changed is that each doubling now adds millions instead of pennies.

The amount on any day follows one formula: 0.01 × 2^(day − 1). The little raised number is the whole story. When a quantity grows by adding, it climbs like a staircase with equal steps. When it grows by multiplying, it starts flat and then rises like a wall. Populations, bank balances, spreading rumors and radioactive samples all follow the multiplying kind of rule. This chapter is about reading, writing and predicting with that rule.
story.think: The million-dollar offer wins for the first 27 days. Why do you think the doubling penny still feels like a trick even after you see the numbers?

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing Powers
lessons.mainIdea: When powers share a base, multiply them by adding the exponents and divide them by subtracting the exponents.
reading: A *power* is a short way to write repeated multiplication. 2^5 means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, which equals 32. The 2 is the *base*, the number being multiplied, and the 5 is the *exponent*, the count of factors. Suppose a computer file doubles in size 3 times, then doubles 4 more times. The size grows by 2^3 and then by 2^4. Written out, that is (2 × 2 × 2) × (2 × 2 × 2 × 2), which is seven 2s in a row, or 2^7 = 128.

That example shows the *product rule*: when you multiply powers with the same base, keep the base and add the exponents. 2^3 × 2^4 = 2^(3 + 4) = 2^7. Check it with numbers: 8 × 16 = 128, and 2^7 = 128. The rule works for any base, including variables: x^2 × x^5 = x^7, and 3a^4 × 5a^2 = 15a^6. Multiply the coefficients (3 × 5 = 15), then add the exponents on a (4 + 2 = 6).

Division goes the other way. 5^6 ÷ 5^2 means six 5s on top and two 5s on the bottom. Two pairs cancel, leaving four 5s: 5^4 = 625. This is the *quotient rule*: keep the base and subtract the exponents. 5^6 ÷ 5^2 = 5^(6 − 2) = 5^4. Check: 15,625 ÷ 25 = 625. With variables, y^9 ÷ y^4 = y^5.

The most common mistake is multiplying the exponents instead of adding them. 2^3 × 2^4 is not 2^12; that would be 4,096, not 128. Another mistake is adding exponents when the bases differ. 2^3 × 5^2 cannot be combined into one power. Just compute it: 8 × 25 = 200. The rules apply only when the bases match.

words.d: a base raised to an exponent, like 2^5, which means 2 multiplied by itself 5 times
the number being multiplied repeatedly in a power; in 2^5 the base is 2
the raised number that counts how many times the base is used as a factor; in 2^5 it is 5
to multiply powers with the same base, keep the base and add the exponents: b^m × b^n = b^(m + n)
to divide powers with the same base, keep the base and subtract the exponents: b^m ÷ b^n = b^(m − n)

look.title: Powers of Ten
look.text: Powers of ten make the rules easy to see. 10^3 = 1,000 and 10^4 = 10,000. Multiply them: 1,000 × 10,000 = 10,000,000, which has seven zeros, so it is 10^7. The product rule says 10^3 × 10^4 = 10^(3 + 4) = 10^7. The zeros simply pile up. Now try division. 10^8 is 100,000,000 (eight zeros) and 10^5 is 100,000 (five zeros).
look.prompt: Use the quotient rule to simplify 10^8 ÷ 10^5. Then divide the actual numbers. Do the zeros agree with the rule?

check.q: Simplify 3^4 × 3^2.
check.why: Same base, so add the exponents: 4 + 2 = 6. Check: 81 × 9 = 729 = 3^6. Multiplying the exponents or the bases is the common error.

check.q: Simplify x^9 ÷ x^3.
check.why: Same base, so subtract the exponents: 9 − 3 = 6, giving x^6. Adding gives x^12 and dividing the exponents gives x^3, both wrong.

check.q: Which expression can NOT be rewritten as a single power using the product or quotient rule?
check.why: 4^2 × 3^2 has two different bases, so the rules do not apply. Just compute it: 16 × 9 = 144. The others share a base.

lessons.title: Powers of Powers and the Zero Exponent
lessons.mainIdea: Raising a power to a power multiplies the exponents, and any nonzero base raised to the zero power equals 1.
reading: Picture a square poster whose side is 2^3 = 8 inches long. Its area is (2^3)^2 = 8 × 8 = 64 square inches. Now count the 2s: 8 × 8 is (2 × 2 × 2) × (2 × 2 × 2), six 2s, so the area is 2^6 = 64. This is the *power rule*: to raise a power to a power, multiply the exponents. (2^3)^2 = 2^(3 × 2) = 2^6. Likewise (x^4)^5 = x^20.

The rule extends to products inside parentheses. (3x^2)^3 means 3x^2 × 3x^2 × 3x^2. Cube the 3 to get 27, and multiply the exponents on x: x^(2 × 3) = x^6. So (3x^2)^3 = 27x^6. A common mistake is writing 3x^6, forgetting to cube the *coefficient*. Every factor inside the parentheses gets the outside exponent.

What does 5^0 mean? Use the quotient rule: 5^3 ÷ 5^3 = 5^(3 − 3) = 5^0. But 5^3 ÷ 5^3 = 125 ÷ 125 = 1. So 5^0 = 1. Any nonzero base raised to the *zero exponent* is 1. Another way to see it: follow the pattern 5^3 = 125, 5^2 = 25, 5^1 = 5. Each step down divides by 5, so the next step is 5 ÷ 5 = 1.

Students often guess 5^0 = 0 because zero means nothing. But the exponent counts factors, and using zero factors of 5 leaves the starting value, 1, the number that leaves multiplication unchanged. Watch the parentheses: 3x^0 = 3 × 1 = 3, but (3x)^0 = 1, because the parentheses put the 3 inside the power.

words.d: to raise a power to a power, multiply the exponents: (b^m)^n = b^(m × n)
the number multiplied in front of a variable, like the 3 in 3x^2
any nonzero base raised to the power 0 equals 1; for example 7^0 = 1

look.title: Stepping Down the Powers
look.text: Write the powers of 3 in a column: 3^4 = 81, 3^3 = 27, 3^2 = 9, 3^1 = 3. Each line is the line above divided by 3: 81 ÷ 3 = 27, 27 ÷ 3 = 9, 9 ÷ 3 = 3. The pattern does not have to stop at 3^1. Keep dividing by 3 to find the next line, and the line after that.
look.prompt: What does the pattern say 3^0 must equal? If you divide by 3 once more, what would 3^(−1) be?

check.q: Simplify (x^4)^3.
check.why: A power of a power multiplies the exponents: 4 × 3 = 12. Adding them gives x^7, which is the product-rule mistake.

check.q: What is 12^0?
check.why: Any nonzero base to the zero power is 1. Check with the quotient rule: 12^2 ÷ 12^2 = 144 ÷ 144 = 1.

check.q: Simplify (2y^3)^4.
check.why: Both factors get the exponent 4: 2^4 = 16 and (y^3)^4 = y^12. Forgetting to raise the 2 gives 2y^12.

lessons.title: Negative Exponents
lessons.mainIdea: A negative exponent means divide: b^(−n) equals 1/b^n, the reciprocal of the positive power.
reading: Continue the pattern from 2^3 = 8, 2^2 = 4, 2^1 = 2, 2^0 = 1. Each step divides by 2. The next step is 1 ÷ 2 = 1/2, then 1/4, then 1/8. So 2^(−1) = 1/2, 2^(−2) = 1/4, 2^(−3) = 1/8. A *negative exponent* does not make a number negative. It tells you to take the *reciprocal*: flip the power into a fraction. 2^(−3) = 1/2^3 = 1/8.

The quotient rule agrees. 4^2 ÷ 4^5 = 4^(2 − 5) = 4^(−3). Written out, 16 ÷ 1,024 = 1/64, and 1/4^3 = 1/64. The same idea works with variables: x^3 ÷ x^7 = x^(−4) = 1/x^4. To write an expression with only positive exponents, move each factor with a negative exponent across the fraction bar and make its exponent positive. So 5x^(−2) = 5/x^2, and 1/y^(−3) = y^3.

Scientists use negative *powers of ten* to write tiny numbers. A red blood cell is about 7 × 10^(−6) meters across. Since 10^(−6) = 1/1,000,000, that is 0.000007 meters. A common mistake is thinking 10^(−6) is a negative number. It is small, not negative: a positive number less than 1.

Two errors to watch. First, (−3)^2 = 9 but 3^(−2) = 1/9; the position of the minus sign changes everything. Second, only the factor with the negative exponent flips. In 3x^(−2), the 3 stays on top: 3/x^2, not 1/(3x^2). The exponent belongs to x alone.

words.d: an exponent below zero; b^(−n) means 1 divided by b^n, so 2^(−3) = 1/8
the flip of a number; the reciprocal of 8 is 1/8 and the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2
10 raised to an exponent; 10^3 = 1,000 and 10^(−3) = 0.001

look.title: Powers of Ten, Up and Down
look.cite: Computed from the definition of powers of 10
look.prompt: Each row is the row above divided by 10. What is 10^(−4) as a decimal, and how many places does the decimal point move from 1?

check.q: What is 3^(−2)?
check.why: A negative exponent means reciprocal: 3^(−2) = 1/3^2 = 1/9. It is positive, not −9.

check.q: Write 4x^(−3) using only positive exponents.
check.why: Only x has the negative exponent, so only x moves to the bottom: 4/x^3. The 4 stays on top.

check.q: Which number equals 10^(−3)?
check.why: 10^(−3) = 1/10^3 = 1/1,000 = 0.001. It is a small positive number, not a negative one.

lessons.title: Rational Exponents and Roots
lessons.mainIdea: An exponent of 1/n means the nth root, so 9^(1/2) = √9 = 3 and 8^(1/3) equals the cube root of 8, which is 2.
reading: A *square root* of a number is a value that, times itself, gives the number. √49 = 7 because 7 × 7 = 49. A *cube root* uses the value three times: the cube root of 27 is 3 because 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. Roots undo powers. Now ask what 9^(1/2) could mean. By the product rule, 9^(1/2) × 9^(1/2) = 9^(1/2 + 1/2) = 9^1 = 9. So 9^(1/2) is a number that, squared, gives 9. That is the square root: 9^(1/2) = √9 = 3.

In general, b^(1/n) is the nth root of b, and b^(m/n) means take the nth root, then raise to the mth power, or the other way around; the order does not matter. Example: 8^(2/3). The cube root of 8 is 2, and 2^2 = 4, so 8^(2/3) = 4. Check by the other order: 8^2 = 64, and the cube root of 64 is 4. Same answer. Another: 16^(3/4). The fourth root of 16 is 2, since 2^4 = 16, and 2^3 = 8.

A *rational exponent* follows all the exponent rules. 4^(1/2) × 4^(3/2) = 4^(4/2) = 4^2 = 16. Check: 2 × 8 = 16. The rules also simplify a *radical*. √72 = √(36 × 2) = √36 × √2 = 6√2, because 36 is the largest *perfect square* that divides 72. Taking the root of each factor separately is the power rule applied to a product.

The most common mistake is reading 8^(1/3) as 8 ÷ 3 or as 8 × 1/3. It is the cube root: 2. Another mistake is 25^(1/2) = 12.5. Halving is not the same as taking a square root; 25^(1/2) = 5. Always ask: what number, multiplied by itself n times, gives the base?

words.d: a number that gives the original when multiplied by itself; √36 = 6 because 6 × 6 = 36
a number used three times as a factor to give the original; the cube root of 64 is 4
an exponent that is a fraction; b^(m/n) means the nth root of b raised to the mth power
an expression with a root sign, like √72 or the cube root of 20
a whole number that is the square of a whole number, such as 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36

look.title: Two Roads to the Same Root
look.text: Find 32^(3/5) two ways. Road one: the fifth root of 32 is 2, since 2^5 = 32, and then 2^3 = 8. Road two: 32^3 = 32,768, and the fifth root of 32,768 is 8, since 8^5 = 32,768. Both roads give 8, but the first road keeps the numbers small. Now try 27^(2/3).
look.prompt: Find 27^(2/3) by taking the cube root first, then by squaring first. Which road is easier, and do you get the same answer?

check.q: What is 64^(1/3)?
check.why: The exponent 1/3 means cube root. 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, so the answer is 4. Dividing by 3 or taking the square root (8) are the common errors.

check.q: What is 27^(2/3)?
check.why: Cube root of 27 is 3, and 3^2 = 9. Multiplying 27 by 2/3 gives 18, which confuses the exponent with a factor.

check.q: Simplify √50.

lessons.title: Doubling and Growth Factors
lessons.mainIdea: Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor each step, so the value after x steps is start × factor^x.
reading: The penny from the chapter story doubles each day. Day 1: $0.01. Day 2: $0.02. Day 3: $0.04. Day 4: $0.08. Each day you multiply by 2, not add 2. After d doublings the amount is 0.01 × 2^d. After 10 doublings, 0.01 × 2^10 = 0.01 × 1,024 = $10.24. After 20, 0.01 × 1,048,576 = $10,485.76. This is *exponential growth*: the same multiplier used again and again.

The general form is y = a × b^x. Here a is the *starting value*, the value when x = 0; b is the *growth factor*, the number you multiply by each step; and x counts the steps. A bacteria colony that starts at 500 cells and triples every hour has y = 500 × 3^x. After 4 hours: 500 × 3^4 = 500 × 81 = 40,500 cells. Check by stepping: 500, 1,500, 4,500, 13,500, 40,500.

Compare with a linear pattern. If the colony gained 500 cells per hour instead, after 4 hours it would have 500 + 4 × 500 = 2,500 cells. Adding the same amount each step is linear; multiplying by the same factor each step is exponential. In a table, linear values have a constant difference and exponential values have a constant *ratio*. The ratio of neighbors in 500, 1,500, 4,500 is 1,500 ÷ 500 = 3 and 4,500 ÷ 1,500 = 3.

A common mistake is computing 500 × 3^4 as (500 × 3)^4 = 1,500^4. The exponent applies only to the growth factor, so evaluate 3^4 first, then multiply by 500. Another mistake is swapping the roles of the two numbers in 2^10: the 2 is what you multiply by, and the 10 is how many times.

words.d: growth by multiplying by the same factor greater than 1 each step, like doubling every day
the value when x = 0, the a in y = a × b^x
the number you multiply by each step, the b in y = a × b^x; doubling has growth factor 2
one value divided by the one before it; exponential tables have a constant ratio

look.title: The Doubling Penny, Day by Day
look.prompt: From day 20 to day 30 there are 10 doublings, so the amount multiplies by 2^10 = 1,024. Check that 5,242.88 × 1,024 matches the last row.

check.q: A population of 200 doubles every year. Which equation gives the population after x years?
check.why: Start at 200 and multiply by 2 for each year: y = 200 × 2^x. Adding 2x is linear, and 200^x puts the wrong number in the base.

check.q: Evaluate 50 × 3^3.
check.why: Do the power first: 3^3 = 27, then 50 × 27 = 1,350. Multiplying first and cubing 150 gives 3,375,000.

check.q: Which list of values shows exponential growth?
check.why: 3, 6, 12, 24 has a constant ratio of 2. The lists 3, 6, 9, 12 and 3, 9, 15, 21 add the same amount, so they are linear.

lessons.title: Percent Growth and Compound Interest
lessons.mainIdea: A rate of r per period gives the growth factor 1 + r, so 5% growth means multiply by 1.05 each period.
reading: Suppose a savings account holds $1,000 and earns 5% *interest* each year, added to the balance. After one year the interest is 0.05 × 1,000 = $50, so the balance is $1,050. Notice that 1,000 + 0.05 × 1,000 = 1,000 × (1 + 0.05) = 1,000 × 1.05. Growing by 5% is the same as multiplying by 1.05. In the second year the 5% is figured on $1,050, so the interest is $52.50 and the balance is $1,102.50. Interest that earns interest is called *compound interest*.

The pattern is y = 1,000 × 1.05^t, where t is the number of years and 1,000 is the *principal*. After 10 years, 1.05^10 ≈ 1.629, so the balance is about $1,629. Simple interest, which pays $50 every year with no compounding, would give 1,000 + 10 × 50 = $1,500. The gap widens over time. The rule for percent growth: the growth factor is 1 + r, where r is the *rate* written as a decimal. A 3% rate gives 1.03, a 12% rate gives 1.12, and a 150% rate gives 2.5.

Some accounts compound more than once a year. The formula A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) splits the yearly rate r among n periods per year. At 6% compounded monthly, each month multiplies by 1 + 0.06/12 = 1.005, and two years hold 24 periods. For $500: 500 × 1.005^24 ≈ 500 × 1.1272 ≈ $563.58. Yearly compounding at 6% would give 500 × 1.06^2 = 500 × 1.1236 = $561.80, a little less.

The most common mistake is using 0.05 as the growth factor. Multiplying by 0.05 shrinks $1,000 to $50; you must multiply by 1.05 to keep the original and add 5%. A second mistake is writing a 5% rate as 1.5. Move the decimal two places: 5% = 0.05, so the factor is 1.05, not 1.5.

words.d: money paid for the use of money, usually a percent of the balance each period
interest computed on the balance including earlier interest, so the balance grows exponentially
the starting amount of money deposited or borrowed
the percent of growth per period, written as a decimal in the growth factor 1 + r

look.title: One Thousand Dollars at 5%
look.cite: Example account: 1,000 × 1.05^t, rounded to the cent
look.prompt: Simple interest would give 1,000 + 50t. How far ahead of simple interest is the compound balance at year 5, and at year 10?

check.q: An investment of $2,000 grows 4% per year. Which expression gives its value after 3 years?
check.why: A 4% rate means the growth factor is 1 + 0.04 = 1.04, used 3 times: 2,000 × 1.04^3. Using 0.04 or 1.4 are the classic decimal slips.

check.q: A city of 40,000 people grows 2% per year. About how many people will it have after 1 year?
check.why: 40,000 × 1.02 = 40,800. The growth alone is 800; adding 2,000 would be a 5% increase.

check.q: What growth factor matches a rate of 7.5% per year?
check.why: 7.5% = 0.075 as a decimal, and the factor is 1 + 0.075 = 1.075. The factor 1.75 would mean 75% growth.

lessons.title: Decay and Half-Life
lessons.mainIdea: Exponential decay multiplies by a factor between 0 and 1 each step, such as 0.5 for each half-life or 0.85 for a 15% loss.
reading: A new car bought for $30,000 loses about 15% of its value each year. Losing 15% leaves 85%, so each year multiplies the value by 0.85. After 1 year: 30,000 × 0.85 = $25,500. After 2 years: 25,500 × 0.85 = $21,675. The formula is y = 30,000 × 0.85^t. This is *exponential decay*: the same fraction disappears each period. The *decay factor* is 1 − r, here 1 − 0.15 = 0.85. After 5 years, 0.85^5 ≈ 0.4437, so the car is worth about $13,311.

Radioactive materials decay with a *half-life*: the time it takes for half of the material to be gone. Iodine-131, used in some medical treatments, has a half-life of about 8 days. Start with 80 milligrams. After 8 days, 40 mg remain. After 16 days, 20 mg. After 24 days, 10 mg. The formula is y = 80 × (1/2)^(t/8), where t is in days. The exponent t/8 counts how many half-lives have passed. At t = 24, the exponent is 3 and (1/2)^3 = 1/8, so 80 × 1/8 = 10 mg.

Doctors use the same idea for medicine in the body. If a 200 mg dose of a drug has a half-life of 6 hours, then 100 mg remain after 6 hours, 50 mg after 12 hours, and 25 mg after 18 hours. To find the amount after 9 hours, the exponent is 9/6 = 1.5, and (1/2)^1.5 ≈ 0.354, so about 71 mg remain. Halving repeatedly never reaches zero; the amount just gets closer and closer to it. On a graph, the curve flattens toward the horizontal axis without touching it.

A common mistake is multiplying by 0.15 for a 15% loss. That computes the amount lost, not the amount left. Subtract from 1 first. Another mistake in half-life problems is using t itself as the exponent instead of t divided by the half-life. Twenty-four days with an 8-day half-life is 3 halvings, not 24.

words.d: shrinking by multiplying by the same factor between 0 and 1 each step
the number you multiply by each step when a quantity shrinks; a 15% loss has decay factor 0.85
the time it takes for half of a decaying quantity to disappear

look.title: The Bouncing Ball
look.text: A rubber ball dropped from 250 cm rebounds to 60% of its previous height on each bounce. After bounce 1 it reaches 250 × 0.6 = 150 cm. After bounce 2, 150 × 0.6 = 90 cm. After bounce 3, 54 cm. After bounce 4, 32.4 cm. The decay factor is 0.6, so the height after n bounces is 250 × 0.6^n.
look.prompt: How high does the ball reach after the 5th bounce? Will it ever reach a height of exactly 0 cm according to the formula?

check.q: A $600 phone loses 20% of its value each year. Which equation gives its value after t years?
check.why: Losing 20% leaves 80%, so the decay factor is 0.8: y = 600 × 0.8^t. Using 0.2 tracks the amount lost, and 1.2 would be growth.

check.q: A sample of 160 grams has a half-life of 5 years. How much remains after 15 years?
check.why: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 half-lives: 160 → 80 → 40 → 20 grams. Using 15 as the number of halvings, or stopping after one, gives the wrong amount.

check.q: What decay factor matches losing 35% each period?
check.why: 1 − 0.35 = 0.65 is the fraction that remains. Multiplying by 0.35 gives the part lost, not the part left.

lessons.title: Geometric Sequences
lessons.mainIdea: A geometric sequence multiplies by the same common ratio each term, so the nth term is a(1) × r^(n − 1).
reading: A gym runs a referral plan: 3 people join the first week, and each week the number of new members is 3 times the week before. Week 1: 3. Week 2: 9. Week 3: 27. Week 4: 81. The list 3, 9, 27, 81, … is a *geometric sequence*. Each *term* comes from multiplying the term before it by the same number, the *common ratio*, here 3. To find the ratio of any geometric sequence, divide any term by the one before it: 27 ÷ 9 = 3.

You can describe the sequence two ways. The *recursive rule* says how to get the next term from the current one: a(n) = 3 × a(n − 1), with a(1) = 3. The *explicit rule* lets you jump straight to any term: a(n) = 3 × 3^(n − 1). Term 6 is 3 × 3^5 = 3 × 243 = 729. Check by stepping from 81: 243, then 729. In general, a(n) = a(1) × r^(n − 1). The exponent is n − 1 because the first term has had zero multiplications.

Ratios can be fractions. The sequence 400, 100, 25, 6.25 has ratio 100 ÷ 400 = 1/4, and its explicit rule is a(n) = 400 × (1/4)^(n − 1). Ratios can be negative: 2, −6, 18, −54 has ratio −3, so the signs alternate. Compare an arithmetic sequence such as 5, 8, 11, 14, which adds 3 each time. Arithmetic sequences are linear patterns; geometric sequences are exponential patterns.

The most common mistake is using r^n instead of r^(n − 1). For 3, 9, 27, …, the formula 3 × 3^n gives 9 for the first term, which is wrong. Test your formula on n = 1 before trusting it. Another mistake is finding the ratio by subtracting: 9 − 3 = 6 is a difference, not a ratio.

words.d: a list of numbers where each term is the previous term times the same number
one number in a sequence; a(4) means the fourth term
the number each term is multiplied by to get the next term in a geometric sequence
a rule that gives the next term from the term before it, plus a starting term
a formula that gives any term directly from its position n, like a(n) = 3 × 2^(n − 1)

look.title: Jumping to the Eighth Term
look.text: The sequence 5, 10, 20, 40, … has first term 5 and common ratio 10 ÷ 5 = 2. Its explicit rule is a(n) = 5 × 2^(n − 1). Test it: a(1) = 5 × 2^0 = 5, and a(3) = 5 × 2^2 = 20. Both match the list. Now find the eighth term two ways: by continuing to double from 40, and by the formula with n = 8.
look.prompt: What is a(8)? Which method would you rather use to find a(20), and why?

check.q: What is the common ratio of 6, 24, 96, 384?
check.why: Divide neighbors: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 96 ÷ 24 = 4. Subtracting 24 − 6 = 18 gives a difference, not a ratio.

check.q: A geometric sequence has a(1) = 2 and r = 5. Which is its explicit rule?
check.why: a(n) = a(1) × r^(n − 1) = 2 × 5^(n − 1). Test n = 1: 2 × 5^0 = 2, correct. The rule 2 × 5^n gives 10 for the first term.

check.q: Find the 5th term of 1, 3, 9, …
check.why: a(5) = 1 × 3^4 = 81. Stepping: 1, 3, 9, 27, 81. Using 3^5 gives 243, the sixth term.

lessons.title: Building a Model From a Table
lessons.mainIdea: To build an exponential model from a table or story, find the starting value at x = 0 and the constant ratio between equal steps.
reading: A biology class counts yeast cells under a microscope every hour and records: hour 0, 40 cells; hour 1, 60; hour 2, 90; hour 3, 135. Is the growth exponential? Check the ratios: 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5, 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5, 135 ÷ 90 = 1.5. The ratio is constant, so yes. The starting value is 40 and the growth factor is 1.5, so the *model* is y = 40 × 1.5^x. Predict hour 6: 40 × 1.5^6 = 40 × 11.390625 ≈ 456 cells.

Sometimes the table skips x = 0. A table shows x = 2, y = 50 and x = 3, y = 100. The ratio is 2. Work backward: at x = 1, y = 25; at x = 0, y = 12.5. So y = 12.5 × 2^x. Check: 12.5 × 2^2 = 50. If the steps in x are bigger than 1, divide carefully. Values of 10 at x = 0 and 90 at x = 2 mean the factor for two steps is 9, so the one-step factor is √9 = 3.

Stories work the same way. A video has 500 views, and views grow 20% per day. The starting value is 500, the growth factor is 1 + 0.20 = 1.2, and the model is y = 500 × 1.2^x. After 3 days: 500 × 1.2^3 = 500 × 1.728 = 864 views. To *interpret* a given model, read its parts. In y = 250 × 0.9^x, the 250 is the start, and the 0.9 means a 10% loss each step, because 1 − 0.9 = 0.10.

A common mistake is using the first value in the table as the starting value even when the table begins at x = 1. Another is checking differences instead of ratios. The yeast table has differences 20, 30, 45, which are not constant, so a line would not fit. Whenever values seem to speed up, test for a *constant ratio*.

words.d: an equation that describes a real situation, like y = 40 × 1.5^x for a growing cell count
to explain what each number in a model means in the situation
the same quotient between every pair of neighboring values, the sign of an exponential pattern

look.title: Yeast Cells Every Hour
look.cite: Example count from the model y = 40 × 1.5^x
look.prompt: Divide each value by the one before it. What do you get each time, and what does the model predict for hour 5?

check.q: A table shows x = 0, y = 8; x = 1, y = 24; x = 2, y = 72. Which model fits?
check.why: The start is 8 and the ratio is 24 ÷ 8 = 3, so y = 8 × 3^x. Check: 8 × 3^2 = 72. The differences 16 and 48 are not constant, so it is not linear.

check.q: In the model y = 900 × 0.7^x, what happens each step?
check.why: A factor of 0.7 keeps 70%, so 1 − 0.7 = 0.3 is lost: a 30% decrease each step.

check.q: A table shows x = 1, y = 30 and x = 2, y = 60. What is the starting value at x = 0?
check.why: The ratio is 2, so step back from x = 1: 30 ÷ 2 = 15. Using 30 as the start is the mistake of ignoring that the table begins at x = 1.

lessons.title: Linear or Exponential?
lessons.mainIdea: Linear growth adds the same amount each step and exponential growth multiplies, so exponential growth eventually outruns any linear growth.
reading: Two job offers. Job A pays $100 the first day and adds $50 each day. Job B pays $1 the first day and doubles each day. On day 5, Job A pays 100 + 4 × 50 = $300 and Job B pays 1 × 2^4 = $16. Job A looks far better. But on day 10, Job A pays 100 + 9 × 50 = $550 and Job B pays 2^9 = $512. On day 12, Job A pays $650 and Job B pays 2^11 = $2,048. From then on, Job B wins by more every day.

This always happens. A *linear function* y = mx + b adds the same amount m each step; m is the *slope*. An *exponential function* y = a × b^x with b > 1 multiplies by b each step, so its increases themselves grow. Doubling from 512 adds 512; doubling from 2,048 adds 2,048. Eventually those jumps are larger than any fixed step, so the exponential function passes the linear one and stays ahead. On a graph, the line rises at a steady slope while the curve bends upward more and more steeply.

To decide which type fits data, compare steps of equal size. The list 5, 8, 11, 14 has a *constant difference* of 3, so it is linear: y = 3x + 5. The list 5, 10, 20, 40 has a constant ratio of 2, so it is exponential: y = 5 × 2^x. The list 5, 8, 13, 20 has neither: the differences 3, 5, 7 grow, and the ratios 1.6, 1.625, 1.54 are not constant. That list is quadratic, a shape you will meet in the last chapter of this unit.

A common mistake is judging by the first few values. Early on, a linear function with a big starting value or a steep slope can be far ahead, as Job A was for 10 days. Look at the long run. Another mistake is calling a pattern exponential because it grows fast. Fast is not the test; a constant ratio is.

a function y = a × b^x that multiplies by the same factor each step
the same amount added between every pair of neighboring values, the sign of a linear pattern
the steady rate of change of a linear function, the m in y = mx + b

look.title: Two Paychecks, Day by Day
look.text: Job A: $100 on day 1, then $50 more each day, so day n pays 100 + 50(n − 1). Job B: $1 on day 1, doubling, so day n pays 2^(n − 1). Day 8: A pays $450, B pays $128. Day 9: A pays $500, B pays $256. Day 10: A pays $550, B pays $512. Day 11: A pays $600, B pays $1,024.
look.prompt: On which day does Job B first pay more than Job A? By day 15, how many times larger is Job B's daily pay than Job A's?

check.q: Which list of values is linear?
check.why: 2, 5, 8, 11 adds 3 each time, a constant difference. The first two lists multiply by 2 and by 3, and the last has neither pattern.

check.q: Plan A pays $20 per week. Plan B starts at $1 per week and triples each week. Which statement is true in the long run?
choices: Plan A always pays more per week
Plan B eventually pays more each week and stays ahead
the two plans pay the same each week after week 3
check.why: Plan B pays 1, 3, 9, 27, 81, … and passes $20 at week 4 (27). Its jumps keep growing while Plan A never changes, so B stays ahead.

check.q: A table has values 4, 12, 36, 108 at x = 0, 1, 2, 3. Which rule fits?
check.why: Each value is 3 times the one before, and the start is 4: y = 4 × 3^x. Check x = 3: 4 × 27 = 108. The differences 8, 24, 72 are not constant, so no line fits.

review.why: Same base, so add the exponents: 5 + 3 = 8. Check: 32 × 8 = 256 = 2^8.
The exponent 1/4 means fourth root, and 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81, so the answer is 3. Dividing by 4 gives 20.25, and 9 is the square root.

review.q: A town of 5,000 people shrinks 4% per year. Which model gives its population after t years?
review.why: Losing 4% leaves 96%, so the decay factor is 1 − 0.04 = 0.96. The factor 1.04 would be growth.
A negative exponent means reciprocal: 5^(−2) = 1/5^2 = 1/25. It is positive.

review.q: A geometric sequence has a(1) = 7 and common ratio 2. What is the 4th term?
review.why: a(4) = 7 × 2^3 = 7 × 8 = 56. Stepping: 7, 14, 28, 56. Using 2^4 gives 112, the fifth term.

review.q: $800 is deposited at 3% per year, compounded yearly. What is the balance after 2 years?
review.why: 800 × 1.03^2 = 800 × 1.0609 = $848.72. Simple interest would give 800 + 2 × 24 = $848.00, slightly less.

review.q: Which list has a constant ratio?
review.why: 1, 4, 16, 64 multiplies by 4 each time. The others add a constant (1 or 2) or are the perfect squares, whose ratios 4, 2.25, 1.78 change.
Square both factors: 5^2 = 25 and (x^3)^2 = x^6. Forgetting to square the 5 gives 5x^6, and adding exponents gives x^5.
